subject: Business Administration
title: IV. Operations and Supply Chain Management

segments.text: Operations management
is concerned with the design, execution, and control of the processes that transform inputs (labour, materials, technology, information) into the goods or services an organization delivers.
Supply chain management

extends that view outward, coordinating the network of suppliers, logistics providers, distributors, and customers through which materials, information, and money flow before and after that transformation takes place. This unit moves from the internal decisions of operations (productivity, process design, capacity, location, layout, inventory) to the external, network-level decisions of supply chain management (strategic fit, drivers, the bullwhip effect, coordination, and technology).
Operations
is the function that actually creates the product or service a customer receives, by transforming inputs into outputs — and that transformation can be
physical
(manufacturing raw material into a finished good),
locational
(transportation, moving something to where it is wanted),
informational
(data processing),
physiological
(healthcare), or
experiential
(entertainment, hospitality) — an important point because it shows operations management applies as much to a hospital or an airline as to a factory.
Productivity
compares outputs with the inputs used to produce them, and is usually expressed as output ÷ input. It can be measured as
single-factor productivity
(output relative to one input, such as labour hours) or
multifactor productivity
(output relative to a combined bundle of inputs — labour, capital, materials). A frequently tested subtlety:
higher output alone does not prove higher productivity
— if inputs grew even faster than output, productivity has actually fallen, even though the raw output number looks larger. Always check the ratio, not just the numerator.
Goods versus services
, another point the syllabus asks to be able to state clearly: services are typically more
intangible
(cannot be touched or inventoried in advance), involve higher
customer contact

(the customer is often present during production itself, unlike a factory where production and consumption are separated in time), and are harder to store — a haircut or a diagnosis cannot be manufactured in advance and held in a warehouse for later sale, unlike a physical good.

blocks.text: .3 Operations Strategy in a Global Environment

segments.text: Operations strategy is the process of deciding how processes, capacity, quality, sourcing, and technology will be organized to support the organization’s overall competitive strategy (recall Porter’s generic strategies from the Management unit above — operations strategy is how those broad strategic choices get translated into concrete process and capacity decisions). It typically converts a small set of
competitive priorities
— cost, quality, speed/delivery, dependability, and flexibility — into specific process and capacity choices.
Two vocabulary terms recur throughout this and the following topics:

items.text: Core competencies
are the distinctive capabilities an organization performs especially well, and which competitors find difficult to imitate — these become the basis of sustainable competitive advantage.
Critical success factors
are the specific areas in which the organization must perform well for its overall strategy to succeed, whether or not that area happens to be a core competency yet.

segments.text: Process strategy decides how work will actually be organized to produce outputs, and the syllabus asks for a spectrum from high-variety/low-volume to low-variety/high-volume production:

items.text: Process-focused (job-shop) systems

handle high product variety and comparatively low volume, using flexible, general-purpose resources that can be reconfigured for different jobs (a custom furniture workshop, a specialized print shop).
Repetitive (assembly-line) systems
sit between the two extremes — a standardized sequence of modules assembled in a fixed flow (an automobile assembly line producing several model variants on the same line).
Product-focused (continuous-flow) systems
handle high volume and low variety, using specialized, dedicated equipment arranged in a fixed flow (an oil refinery, a bottling plant).
Mass customization

attempts to combine the best of both extremes — achieving product variety approaching that of a job shop, at a cost and speed approaching that of continuous, high-volume production — typically enabled by modular design and flexible, reconfigurable technology.

segments.text: Process maps and flow diagrams

— visual representations of the sequence of steps a process goes through — are the standard practical tool for identifying delay, duplication, and bottlenecks in an existing process, and are a natural bridge into the next topic.

Business process re-engineering (BPR) means the fundamental, radical redesign of a major business process — typically examined end-to-end, from the original customer need through to the delivered result — in order to achieve dramatic improvements in cost, quality, service, or speed. The critical distinguishing feature, and a frequently tested point, is that BPR asks whether the entire process should be
redesigned from the ground up

, rather than merely improved incrementally step by step, which is the domain of continuous improvement approaches instead. Re-engineering is therefore higher-risk and higher-reward than incremental improvement: it can produce order-of-magnitude gains, but it also disrupts established roles, systems, and routines far more severely, and carries a correspondingly higher risk of implementation failure.
Three related capacity concepts must be kept distinct:

items.text: Design capacity
is the theoretical maximum output rate achievable under ideal conditions.
Effective capacity
is the maximum output realistically achievable given practical constraints (maintenance schedules, quality requirements, scheduling difficulty) — always less than or equal to design capacity.
Actual output
is what was really produced, which may fall further below effective capacity due to unplanned disruptions.

segments.text: From these,
utilization
= actual output ÷ design capacity, and
efficiency
= actual output ÷ effective capacity — note the different denominators, a distinction the exam frequently probes.
A
bottleneck

is the process stage whose limited capacity constrains the flow of the entire system — the overall system’s capacity can never exceed its slowest, most constrained stage, no matter how much spare capacity exists elsewhere.
The single-product break-even formula is:
Q = Fixed Cost ÷ (Price − Variable Cost per unit)
where (Price − Variable Cost per unit) is the
contribution margin per unit
— the amount each unit sold contributes toward covering fixed costs, after its own variable cost is deducted.
Worked example:

A small bakery has fixed monthly costs (rent, basic salaried staff) of Rs 60,000. Each cake sells for Rs 500 and has a variable cost (ingredients, packaging) of Rs 300, giving a contribution margin of Rs 200 per cake. Break-even quantity Q = 60,000 ÷ 200 = 300 cakes per month — below 300 cakes, the bakery makes a loss; above 300, each additional cake contributes Rs 200 toward profit.

Location is a long-term, high-switching-cost decision, because relocating a facility is expensive and disruptive, and location choices directly affect access to customers, labour, suppliers, transportation networks, utilities, operating costs, risk exposure, and regulatory environment.
Manufacturing location
decisions often weigh cost and logistics factors most heavily (transportation cost to move materials in and finished goods out, land and labour cost);
service location

decisions typically weight customer access and local demand more heavily, since many services must be produced close to, or in the presence of, the customer. Location alternatives are typically compared using both
quantitative methods
(cost comparisons, the weighted-factor rating method, the centre-of-gravity method for minimizing transport distance) and
qualitative factors
(political stability, regulatory environment, quality of life for staff) that resist simple numerical comparison but still materially affect the decision.
Layout decisions arrange people, machines, departments, and material movement within a facility, and the choice of layout should follow directly from the process strategy chosen above:

items.text: Product/line layout
arranges resources in the sequence that production actually follows — suited to product-focused, high-volume, low-variety operations.
Process/functional layout

groups similar activities or equipment together (all X-ray machines in one area of a hospital, all lathes in one area of a workshop) — suited to process-focused, high-variety, low-volume operations, since it gives flexibility to route different jobs through the equipment they specifically need.
Fixed-position layout
keeps the product stationary while people, equipment, and materials move to it — used when the product is too large or immobile to move (shipbuilding, major construction projects, aircraft assembly).
Cellular layout

groups the resources needed to produce a family of similar products or tasks into a self-contained “cell,” combining some of the flow efficiency of product layout with some of the flexibility of process layout for moderate-variety, moderate-volume production.

segments.text: Inventory serves as a buffer against uncertainty and supports smooth operations, but it also ties up working capital and creates holding, storage, and obsolescence costs — inventory management is fundamentally about balancing these two competing pressures. Three inventory types are commonly distinguished:

items.text: Cycle inventory
arises simply from ordering or producing in batches rather than continuously (the average inventory level that results from replenishing in periodic lots).
Safety stock
is extra inventory held specifically to protect against uncertainty in demand or supply lead time.
Pipeline (in-transit) inventory
is inventory that has left one location but has not yet arrived at the next — goods currently on a truck or ship, for example.

segments.text: EOQ finds the order quantity that minimizes the sum of ordering costs (which fall as order size increases, since fewer orders are placed per year) and holding costs (which rise as order size increases, since larger average inventory must be held) under a set of simplifying assumptions (constant, known demand; constant lead time; no quantity discounts):
EOQ = √(2DS / H)
where D is annual demand, S is the fixed cost per order, and H is the annual holding cost per unit.
Beyond the order quantity itself, the
reorder point
— when to place the next order — depends on expected demand during the supplier’s lead time, plus any safety stock held to protect against uncertainty in that demand or lead time; a higher desired
service level

(the probability of not running out of stock before the next delivery arrives) requires holding more safety stock, at a higher holding cost — another direct cost/service trade-off, echoing the efficiency/responsiveness trade-off that recurs throughout this unit.

blocks.text: .10 Introduction to Supply Chain Management and Logistics

segments.text: A
supply chain
encompasses the flows of materials, information, and money connecting upstream suppliers all the way through to final customers.
Logistics

is specifically the movement- and storage-focused part of that broader system — transportation, warehousing, and materials handling — and it is important to keep the two terms distinct: logistics is a part of supply chain management, not a synonym for the whole supply chain (a frequently tested point of confusion). Materials generally flow
downstream
(from raw-material supplier toward the final customer); information and money, by contrast, typically flow in
both directions

(a customer order flows upstream as information, while payment flows upstream as money, even as the physical product flows downstream). Supply-chain decisions are conventionally organized across three planning horizons:
strategic
(long-term network design — how many facilities, where),
planning/tactical
(medium-term — quarterly production and inventory plans), and
operational
(short-term, day-to-day scheduling and order fulfilment).

blocks.text: .11 Supply Chain Performance and Strategic Fit

segments.text: Strategic fit

means the supply chain’s actual capabilities are matched to the competitive needs of the specific product and customer being served — there is no single “best” supply chain design in the abstract; the right design depends on the nature of demand and the promise being made to the customer. This is captured in the trade-off between:

items.text: Efficient supply chains
, optimized for low cost and high utilization — best suited to predictable, stable demand (a staple grocery item).
Responsive supply chains
, optimized for speed, flexibility, and the ability to handle demand uncertainty — best suited to unpredictable, fast-changing demand (a fashion item with a short selling season).

segments.text: A frequent, exam-relevant error is designing an efficient (low-cost) supply chain for a product with genuinely unpredictable demand, or a highly responsive (higher-cost) supply chain for a stable, predictable product — in both cases the supply chain design does not match what the product and customer actually need, destroying rather than creating value.
Six major drivers, each involving a trade-off between responsiveness and efficiency, shape overall supply chain performance:

items.text: Facilities

— the physical locations where product is stored, assembled, or fabricated; more facilities generally improve responsiveness (closer to customers) at the cost of efficiency (higher fixed costs, more dispersed inventory).
Inventory
— more inventory improves availability and responsiveness but ties up working capital and increases holding cost (echoing the inventory-management trade-off above).
Transportation
— faster transportation modes improve responsiveness but cost more; slower modes are cheaper but less responsive.
Information

— improves visibility and coordination across the chain, generally improving both efficiency and responsiveness simultaneously when used well (one of the few drivers not involving a direct trade-off).
Sourcing
— the decision of who performs which activities (in-house versus outsourced, single versus multiple suppliers) shapes both cost and flexibility.
Pricing

— pricing strategy can itself shape the pattern of customer demand (promotional pricing, for example, shifts demand timing), directly affecting how much responsiveness or efficiency the rest of the chain needs to provide.

blocks.text: .13 Balancing Supply and Demand: the Bullwhip Effect

segments.text: The
bullwhip effect

describes how relatively small changes in actual customer demand can become progressively amplified into much larger order fluctuations as they move upstream through the supply chain, from retailer to distributor to manufacturer to raw-material supplier. Recognized causes include:

items.text: Forecast updating

— each party in the chain updates its own forecast based on the orders it receives from the party immediately downstream, rather than on the true underlying end-customer demand, compounding any noise or overreaction at each step.
Order batching

— parties order in batches (to save on ordering costs, echoing EOQ above) rather than continuously, creating lumpy order patterns that look like larger demand swings than actually exist at the retail level.
Price promotions and shortage gaming

— a temporary price promotion causes a temporary demand spike that upstream parties may misread as a permanent trend, over-ordering in response; conversely, when a shortage is feared, downstream buyers may order more than they actually need (“gaming”) to secure supply, further distorting the true demand signal upstream.

segments.text: Worked illustration:

a retailer notices a small, genuine 5% rise in weekly sales and, wanting a buffer, increases its order to the distributor by 15% “just in case.” The distributor, seeing what looks like a much stronger 15% demand increase, orders 30% more from the manufacturer to be safe. The manufacturer, in turn, may over-react even further — a small, real 5% signal has been amplified into an enormous swing by the time it reaches the top of the chain, even though the actual end-customer demand barely moved.
Remedies

center on breaking the causes just listed: sharing actual point-of-sale demand data directly across the chain (so upstream parties react to real demand rather than to distorted orders), reducing batch sizes, and aligning incentives so that no single party benefits from over-ordering.
Coordination means aligning decisions and incentives across otherwise-independent supply-chain partners, each of whom may have different, even conflicting, objectives.
Local optimization

— where one member of the chain improves its own individual performance (say, minimizing its own inventory cost) in a way that actually harms total chain performance (by causing stockouts or forecast distortion elsewhere) — is the central obstacle coordination tries to overcome, and is closely related to the bullwhip effect discussed above. Remedies include shared information systems, incentive alignment (structuring contracts so that what benefits one party also benefits the chain as a whole), aligned forecasting processes, joint planning, and clearly agreed service-level expectations between partners.

blocks.text: .15 Information Technology, CRM, and Risk in Supply Chains

segments.text: Information technology

supports supply chain visibility by collecting, processing, and sharing data across the various activities of the chain — but its value depends entirely on the data being timely and accurate, and on the technology being genuinely integrated with actual operational decision-making; technology alone cannot fix an underlying process design flaw or a set of misaligned incentives (a point worth stating explicitly, since it is easy to overstate technology’s power in isolation from the organizational and process issues discussed throughout this unit).
Customer Relationship Management (CRM)

combines customer data, processes, and interaction history so an organization can more consistently acquire, serve, retain, and understand its customers — connecting operations and supply chain decisions back to the customer-facing concerns developed further in the Marketing unit below.
Supply-chain risk management

identifies vulnerabilities (supplier failure, transport disruption, demand volatility, quality problems, cyber incidents, or broader external shocks such as natural disasters or geopolitical disruption), assesses the likelihood and potential impact of each, and selects an appropriate combination of responses — supplier diversification, strategic buffers (inventory or capacity held in reserve), improved visibility, contingency plans, and flexible capacity — to build resilience against the risks judged most significant.
Key takeaways for the Operations and Supply Chain Management unit

items.text: Productivity is a ratio (output/input), not simply a raw output number — always check whether inputs moved as much as, or more than, output before concluding productivity rose.

Design capacity, effective capacity, and actual output are three distinct benchmarks, giving two distinct ratios (utilization and efficiency) with different denominators — a frequently tested distinction.

The efficiency/responsiveness trade-off recurs throughout this unit in different guises: cost-based location vs. customer-access location, inventory holding cost vs. stockout risk, and — at the whole-supply-chain level — efficient chains vs. responsive chains, matched to strategic fit with the specific product’s demand pattern.

The bullwhip effect (demand amplification moving upstream) and local optimization (individually rational decisions that harm total chain performance) are the two central coordination failures this unit’s remedies — information sharing, incentive alignment, joint planning — are designed to address.
